query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting long, explicit ab initio molecular‐dynamics evaluations with a hybrid approach that uses short trajectory sampling combined with covariance‐based extraction of vibrational entropy (supported by machine‐learned interatomic potentials) will yield free energies (and hence fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties) of both solid and fluid states that are comparable in fidelity to full AIMD/TOR-TILD methods, at a substantially reduced computational cost.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental, binary, or multicomponent high‐temperature systems (e.g., high‐entropy alloys or fusion-relevant materials) in their solid and liquid states near fusion temperatures.
generation.intervention: Replace cost‐intensive explicit AIMD/TOR-TILD free-energy evaluations with a surrogate method that (a) rapidly generates short simulation ensembles using ML-trained potentials, and (b) applies a covariance-based (Gaussian) analysis of atomic displacements to compute vibrational entropy and related anharmonic corrections.
generation.conditions: Temperature ranges spanning the fusion transition where both the solid and fluid free energies (including vibrational and anharmonic contributions) need to be accurately resolved. The method is to be tested on systems where atomic displacements remain within a near-Gaussian regime, typical of high-temperature but not extremely anharmonic conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The covariance matrix of atomic displacements, which encapsulates vibrational modes and short-scale ordering in the material.
generation.mechanism: By sampling only short, statistically representative trajectories using ML-driven potentials, the covariance of atomic displacements can be used to accurately extract vibrational entropy—even including some anharmonic effects—without requiring lengthy thermodynamic integration. This surrogate method leverages the assumption that atomic fluctuations remain approximately Gaussian, thereby capturing the essential entropy contributions for both solid and fluid states.
generation.predicted_outcome: The proposed method will reproduce phase free energies, fusion temperatures, and derived thermodynamic observables within acceptable error margins (~5% or better) compared to explicit AIMD or TOR-TILD calculations while reducing computational cost by roughly one to two orders of magnitude.
generation.baseline: Current explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD workflows that require extensive sampling to obtain free energies with full inclusion of vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron-vibration coupling effects.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to work well when the underlying atomic displacement distributions are nearly Gaussian (i.e. when deviations from harmonicity are moderate). In systems with extreme anharmonicity or where non-Gaussian behavior predominates, the method’s accuracy may deteriorate.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the method’s performance in highly anharmonic or extremely multicomponent high-entropy systems where short-range correlations or non-Gaussian displacement distributions become significant. Further benchmarking across diverse material systems is needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative high-temperature system (such as BCC Ti or a Ni-based high-entropy alloy) and compute its free energy over a range of temperatures covering the fusion transition using both the proposed covariance-based (ML-accelerated short trajectory) method and a conventional explicit AIMD/TOR-TILD workflow. Apply identical simulation cell sizes and comparable sampling protocols for direct comparison.
measurements: Calculated free energy values for solid and liquid states
Derived vibrational entropy and other entropy contributions
Fusion (phase-transition) temperatures and related thermodynamic observables
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the free energies (and derived properties such as fusion temperatures) obtained via the covariance-based method deviate by more than an acceptable tolerance (e.g., >5% error) from those obtained by explicit AIMD/TOR-TILD methods, or if the computational cost reduction is not demonstrably significant (e.g., less than a 10x improvement) while maintaining fidelity.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe vibrational entropy of a solid at finite temperature is investigated from the perspective of information theory. Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations generate ensembles of atomic configurations at finite temperature from which we obtain the N-body distribution of atomic displacements, ρN. We calculate the information-theoretic entropy from the expectation value of lnρN. At a first level of approximation, treating individual atomic displacements independently, our method may be applied using Debye–Waller B-factors, allowing diffraction experiments to obtain an upper bound on the thermodynamic entropy. At the next level of approximation we correct the overestimation through inclusion of displacement covariances. We apply this approach to elemental body-centered cubic sodium and face-centered cubic aluminum, showing good agreement with experimental values above the Debye temperatures of the metals. Below the Debye temperatures, we extract an effective vibrational density of states from eigenvalues of the covariance matrix, and then evaluate the entropy quantum mechanically, again yielding good agreement with experiment down to low temperatures. This quantum model is harmonic in the sense that it is exact for quadratic potentials U, but it incorporates anharmonicity through the effective vibrational frequencies which were derived from the simulated covariance matrix. Errors due to applying the quantum harmonic model should be small at low temperatures, where motion generically becomes harmonic. Some prior studies employ time-dependent velocity correlation functions, then Fourier transform over time to obtain frequencies [,,]. The systematics of that approach differ markedly from ours, as in principle we do not require time evolution at all; we only simulate trajectories for the sake of enlarging our configurational ensemble. The model Hamiltonian can be constructed in the actual harmonic limit of small oscillations by evaluating the force constants within density functional perturbation theory. This mode substantially underestimates the high temperature entropy as it neglects thermal expansion. The quasiharmonic approximation can be used to predict thermal expansion, resulting in improved agreement, or better yet we can evaluate the force constants at the experimental lattice parameters. The method applies generally to solids, but the particular implementation given here relies on the accuracy of a Gaussian approximation to the distribution function. Hence it is most likely to work when the atomic displacements are small, and it is likely to fail in molecular solids where coherent bond rotations are present. Although we mainly demonstrated the method for elemental solids, it also holds in principle for complex crystalline and noncrystalline solids. We give an example of such an application for the MoNbTaW high entropy alloy. The quasiharmonic method may be equally accurate and more efficient than our AIMD method when anharmonicity mainly enters through thermal expansion, but a simulation-based approach in principle includes additional anharmonic contributions. Doing so may require correlations beyond those captured by the Gaussian approximation (see Section 3.3.1). Our simulation-based approach seems most useful when the simulation has already been completed for other purposes. Then, the entropy comes essentially for free on top of whatever other information was sought.
